Presenter 1 • 45 seconds

Good day, panelists and adviser. We are Evon Christian Pahugot Vergara, Justin Comendador, and Xymmer James Nadera. Our system is Kodigo, a point-of-sale and inventory application for small retail operations. The complete research title appears here as recorded in our manuscript. Today we will explain the operational problem, the architecture, and the mechanisms that connect checkout with inventory and reporting. After this presentation, we will demonstrate those workflows in the application. We will distinguish what the repository implements from what still requires deployment or evaluation evidence. name: text-27
text: Design response: connect sales, stock movements, and reporting through stored records

Presenter 1 • 65 seconds

The manuscript frames the problem around fragmented records in small and medium enterprises, especially where sales and stock monitoring depend on separate manual steps. A sale can appear in one record while the stock record still needs an update. Across branches, that separation makes reconciliation harder and delays the information available to an owner. The four links on this slide summarize that problem: recording work, stock visibility, inconsistent records, and reporting delay. They are a synthesis of the manuscript, rather than measured improvement claims about Kodigo. We are not claiming that the system has already reduced errors by a particular percentage. The design response is to connect recorded sales with stock movements and derive reports from those stored records.

Presenter 1 • 70 seconds

Our manuscript states a general objective to design, develop, and evaluate a cloud-based inventory and financial management framework tailored for small and medium enterprises. We have condensed its three specific objectives here. First, identify the operational bottlenecks in manual tracking and reconciliation. That research context informs the connected POS and inventory workflow. Second, determine the appropriate system framework and information security measures. In the implementation, we can point to authentication, assigned-store access, and database validation. Third, evaluate acceptability in terms of cost-effectiveness, reliability, efficiency, and security. The existing system and testing material support evaluation, but they do not establish a completed acceptability score. The final research wording should still receive adviser approval, particularly because the application provides operational financial reporting rather than a full accounting system.

Presenter 1 • 65 seconds

The implemented scope covers sales, product and stock control, replenishment and suppliers, monitoring and reports, and user administration. The POS includes receipts and transaction history, with controlled void and refund workflows. Inventory supports configured receiving units and selling options that relate to base stock. Purchasing includes supplier records and purchase orders. Consignment records track received stock and supplier balances, including payments or credits entered by an Admin. Reports and descriptive analytics use recorded activity. Access differs by role and assigned store, so these capabilities are not available to every user. The next part will show how the application separates interface behavior from the backend operations that preserve records. I will now hand over to Presenter 2 for the technical architecture.

Presenter 2 • 90 seconds

Kodigo is a React and TypeScript browser application built with Vite. Tailwind and Radix support the interface. Zustand manages application state such as the cart and active store, while TanStack Query actively manages reporting and other query data. The browser uses the Supabase client directly. Authentication belongs to Supabase Auth. Table access passes through the Data API and row policies, while important transactions call PostgreSQL functions through RPC. Two Edge Functions handle privileged account management and invite generation. Storage supports uploaded assets. PostgreSQL holds authoritative business records and runs validation, stock triggers, and reporting queries. IndexedDB stores a local product cache and bounded queues, and reconnect events attempt replay. A queued sale is not yet proof of a database commit. Vercel SPA rewrite configuration exists in the repository, although this diagram does not establish the live hosting state. Optional receipt printing uses browser/PDF output and a QZ Tray bridge for supported hardware.

name: text-96

Presenter 2 • 80 seconds

This diagram deliberately shows a small set of real table names. A product can have several selling options, but the current sale path deducts the required quantity from the product’s base stock. A sale contains multiple sale_items. Each line identifies its product and can identify a configured selling option. Stock receiving writes restock_history, and stock operations create inventory_movements with before-and-after quantities. The solid relationships on this slide represent product or sale references, with one-to-many labels for clarity. Store scope and user membership also exist through stores, profiles, and store_users, but those entities are omitted here to keep the diagram readable. Sale lines and receipt records preserve historical values so later product edits do not simply replace the values used to describe a past sale. Reports combine these persisted records and snapshots rather than relying only on what the cart currently displays.

name: text-105
text: process_pos_sale_v4 calls v3. Row locks and exceptions protect the transaction.

name: text-111
text: Illustrative arithmetic only. The stock-deduction trigger uses the configured multiplier.

name: text-113
text: Receiving separates stock from price approval

name: text-117
text: receive_product_stock calls the receiving function. An authorized action applies a price change.

Presenter 2 • 100 seconds

Three mechanisms are central. First, online checkout calls process_pos_sale_v4, which delegates the underlying sale work to version three and adds validation of line discounts. The database checks the authenticated user, role, store assignment, stock, prices, and submitted totals. It locks product rows so concurrent requests cannot both consume the same available quantity. Sale rows, line items, payment and receipt information, and the triggered stock changes belong to the database transaction. An exception rolls that transaction back. The wrapper can also return a prior committed result for the same sale ID and cashier. Second, stock conversion is deterministic: selling two packs of six consumes twelve base units. The example is illustrative, not a recorded test result. Third, receiving converts configured delivery quantities into base units, records cost and stock history, and prepares a suggested price. An authorized user reviews price changes separately. These rules are inspectable arithmetic and validation, which suit repeatable retail operations without requiring machine learning.

Presenter 2 • 80 seconds

The four roles have different responsibilities. Admin operates within assigned stores. Cashier uses the POS and the permitted transaction tools. Inventory maintains product and stock information and can use inventory-oriented reports. Super Admin currently manages invite codes through a separate portal, rather than acting as a general store operator. The frontend hides or redirects unavailable routes, but that is only one layer. SQL policies and protected functions also check role and store membership. The account-management Edge Function checks the caller before using privileged backend credentials. TOTP enrollment is supported, and the MFA policy requires AAL2 for accounts with a verified factor. We should not describe this as a completed penetration test or security certification. The repository also contains a proposed Super Admin access change in a drafts folder. That proposal is excluded from this matrix. Presenter 3 will now explain the testing evidence and our demonstration plan.

Presenter 3 • 75 seconds

The manuscript names Agile Scrum and describes planning, design, development, testing, deployment, and review. The repository contains incremental implementation and a CI workflow, but source files alone do not verify sprint ceremonies or completed user acceptance. For this pre-defense package, seven local unit tests passed. They cover reporting allocations, refunds, partial captures, date boundaries, monthly rankings, hardware-action separation, and historical base-unit prices. TypeScript and ESLint also completed successfully. These are narrow engineering checks, not a total-system success rate. The integration harness includes checkout, stock, and store-isolation scenarios, but it creates and removes test records. We did not run it against a database during this task. The CI workflow can also skip that stage when it is not enabled. Live transaction, RLS, MFA, and intended-user evaluation remain separate evidence to collect in an approved test environment.

text: Validation target: persisted transaction, matching stock arithmetic, reports from recorded activity

Presenter 3 • 80 seconds

This is our proposed live demonstration sequence, not a claim that the backend has already been cleared. An authorized operator must prepare an approved demonstration environment, preserve the schema and required authentication and configuration, and independently verify that business records are empty. A store Admin account must remain available because the current Super Admin interface cannot perform ordinary store setup. Preparation must also account for browser queues, since old queued writes could repopulate cleared records. During the demonstration, we will log in, create a synthetic product with zero opening stock, and receive a configured package quantity. We will process a cash sale, refresh inventory, and compare the stock change with the recorded sale and movement history. Finally, we will use the matching store, date range, and report filters to reconcile the totals. The checklist includes an illustrative package example and recovery steps if connectivity or printing fails.

name: text-185
text: Configured conversions and recorded consumption support explainable stock decisions. No AI/ML claim.

Presenter 3 • 65 seconds

The application is online-first. It has a cache and selected queues, but it does not provide comprehensive offline reporting or automatic conflict resolution. Replay failures remain stored with an error status, so reconnection alone does not guarantee that every operation has committed. We still need evidence that the deployed migration chain, role policies, and critical workflows match this repository. Descriptive analytics and replenishment calculations use recorded activity, lead time, and configured buffers. They are rule-based calculations, not predictive machine learning. That choice makes conversion and stock decisions easier to explain and audit for the current requirements. Future work could strengthen queue recovery and concurrent-operation testing. Receipt OCR or demand forecasting may be considered later, subject to approval and evaluation. They are not current features. The system also does not replace certified accounting software, tax filing, or a supplier-facing portal.

Presenter 3 • 45 seconds

Kodigo connects checkout with stock movements and operational reports for assigned retail stores. Its main technical contributions are database-validated transactions, configured base-unit conversion, and access controls that extend beyond the interface. The repository and local checks give us a basis for evaluation, while live deployment and end-to-end behavior still need direct validation. We will now move to the application and follow the prepared sequence. As we demonstrate, we will compare the recorded sale, resulting stock, and report values so the panel can inspect whether the actual behavior matches the design we have explained.
